passages.original: quamobrem et mcritis et gradibus longe dispares ausus est definire. Hujus igitur error ad confutationem Sabellianæ impietatis proficiat, audiatque Sa- bellius in tantum Patris et Filii ct Spiritus sancti tres esse personas, ut cos Arius et potestate dissimiles et nalura diversos audeat profiteri. Audiat rursus hic idem Arius, in tantum Patrem et Filium, et Spiritum samtum unius potestatis, uniusque esse naturae, ut Sabellius unam eorum dicat esse personam.
passages.english: For this reason he also dared to define them as widely unequal both in merits and in degrees. Let this man's error, then, serve to refute the Sabellian impiety, and let Sabellius hear that the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are three persons to such an extent that Arius dares to profess them both unlike in power and different in nature. Let this same Arius in turn hear that the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are of one power and of one nature to such an extent that Sabellius says they are one person.

passages.original: ita tamen ut ipso illo utriusque genens sermone nunquam nisi cum significatione et hominis locutus et Dei sit. Ecce aperte communionem utrarumque docens naturarum, et Verbum dixit loqui et agere quæ carnis sunt, et carnem quæ Verbi sunt. Cui sententiæ et beatus quoque congruens Ambrosius ita dicit (Lib. II de Fide ad Gratianum, cap. 4, initio) : Consors utriusque naturæ, id est humanæ atque divinæ, in natura hominis subiit passionem; ut indiscrete et Dominus majestatis dicatur esse qui passus est, et filius hominis, sicut scriptum est, qui descendit de cœlo. Perspicue nimis et communionem operis, et proprietatem utriusque naturae descripsit : dum et carnem propter Verbum de coelo descendisse, et Verbum propter carnem mortem subiisse divina testantur eloquia;
passages.english: yet in such a way that in that very speech of both kinds he never spoke except with the signification both of man and of God. See how, plainly teaching the communion of both natures, he has said both that the Word speaks and does the things that belong to the flesh, and that the flesh [speaks and does] the things that belong to the Word. Agreeing with this view, the blessed Ambrose also says this (Book II On the Faith, to Gratian, ch. 4, at the beginning): "Sharing in both natures, that is, human and divine, he underwent the passion in the nature of man, so that without distinction both he who suffered is called the Lord of majesty, and the Son of Man, as it is written, is he who came down from heaven." He has described very clearly both the communion of operation and the property of each nature, since the divine oracles testify both that the flesh came down from heaven on account of the Word, and that the Word underwent death on account of the flesh;

passages.original: Item dixit Leo (Num 4) : Esurire, sitire, lassescere atque dormire, evidenter humanum est: et non est ejusdem natum flere miserationis affectu amicum mortuum, et eumdem ad vocis imperium excitare redivivum. Hoc et beatus Gregorius Nazianzenus episcopus asseruit, dicens (Orat. 38 in Christi Nativitatem, post medium) : Cum ergo processisset ex Virgine Deus, in ea quam assumpserat, humana natura, unum e duobus in invicem contrariis existens, carne ac spiritu, aliud in Deum assumitur, aliud 80 Deitatis gratiam praestat.
passages.english: Likewise Leo said (no. 4): "To hunger, to thirst, to grow weary and to sleep is evidently human; and it does not belong to the same [nature] to weep with the feeling of pity for a dead friend, and, by the command of the voice, to raise the same man to life again." The blessed Gregory Nazianzen, the bishop, also asserted this, saying (Oration 38 on the Nativity of Christ, after the middle): "When, therefore, God had come forth from the Virgin in the human nature which he had assumed, being one out of two things contrary to each other, flesh and spirit, the one is taken up into God, the other bestows the grace of Deity."
passages.notes: "natum" read as "naturae"; "80" is a stray page number from the edition, omitted.

passages.original: non quia in corruptionem ceciderat (absit), sed quia ejus resurrexit corpus. Ita Christum hominem (quem tamen et Deum confitemur) non tanquam hominem cum Verbo coadorantes, ne divisionis quædam species inducatur, sed unum jam et eumdem adorantes. Hoc et beatus Hilarius paucis explicat verbis. Videsne , inquit (Lib. IX de Trinit., noti longe ab initio), ita Deum et hominem prædicari, ut mors homini, Deo rero, carnis excitatio deputetur ? Naturam Dei in virtute resurrectionis intellige, dispensationem hominis in morte cognosce: et cum sint utraque utriusque gesta naturis, unum tamen Jesum eum memento esse qui utrumque est.
passages.english: not because it had fallen into corruption (far from it), but because his body rose again. Thus [we worship] Christ the man (whom nevertheless we also confess as God), not worshipping him as a man together with the Word, lest some appearance of division be introduced, but worshipping [him] now as one and the same. The blessed Hilary too explains this in a few words. "Do you see," he says (Book IX On the Trinity, not far from the beginning), "that God and man are so proclaimed that death is assigned to the man, but to God the raising of the flesh? Understand the nature of God in the power of the resurrection, recognise the dispensation of the man in the death; and though both deeds were done by their respective natures, remember nevertheless that he who is both is one Jesus."
passages.notes: "rero" read as "vero", "noti" as "non". The opening sentence lacks a main verb in the Latin; "[we worship]" supplied.

passages.original: 35) in homilia de Ascensiono Domini, ita dicit: Deus nobis juxte irascebatur, et nos contemnebamus iratum, et clementem Dominum decli- nabamus: et se medium Christus ingessit, et sociavit utramque naturam, et nobis quod imminebat supplicium ipse sustinuit. Item : cognoscamus igitur quæ na- Iura est, cui dixit : Sede ad dexteram meam, et esto meæ particeps sedis: illa nimitum natura quæ audierat : Terra es, et in terram ibis. Hoc et Augustinus sentiens, Gratulandum, inquit (Tract. 78 in Joannem), fuerat humanæ naturæ, eo quod sic assumpta est a Deo Verbo, ut immortalis constituereturin cœlo; atque ita fieret terra sublimis, ut incorruptibilis sederet ad dexteram Patris.
passages.english: 35), in the homily on the Ascension of the Lord, says this: "God was justly angry with us, and we despised him in his anger, and turned away from the merciful Lord; and Christ placed himself in the middle, and joined both natures together, and himself bore the punishment that hung over us." Likewise: "Let us recognise, therefore, what nature it is to which he said: Sit at my right hand, and be a sharer of my throne: namely that nature which had heard: Earth you are, and into earth you shall go." Augustine too, holding this view, says (Tractate 78 on John): "Human nature had cause to rejoice, in that it was so assumed by God the Word as to be set immortal in heaven, and so earth became exalted, that, incorruptible, it might sit at the right hand of the Father."
passages.notes: Passage begins mid-citation (reference to Chrysostom, tom. V, serm. 35). "nimitum" read as "nimirum".
